title: Dense and sparse computation
summary: A sparse expert model separates how much knowledge is stored from how much computation each token activates.

sections.title: Every token need not use every weight
paragraphs: In a dense Transformer, each token passes through the same feed-forward network at a given layer. A sparse mixture-of-experts layer provides several candidate networks and routes each token to a subset. Sparsity here describes conditional execution of expert modules, not necessarily zero-valued weights inside their matrices. Attention and other shared components can remain dense. The routing decision is part of the learned computation and may differ across tokens within one sentence.

sections.title: Distinguish arithmetic from storage
paragraphs: Suppose an MoE layer contains eight experts, each with ten million parameters, and selects two experts per token. It stores eighty million expert parameters but uses twenty million of them for that token, ignoring router and shared components. This can increase parameter capacity without multiplying per-token expert arithmetic by eight. It does not make the remaining sixty million parameters disappear: they still require storage somewhere and may require movement across devices depending on the deployment.
sections.formula: P_expert,total = E × P_expert; P_expert,active ≈ k × P_expert

sections.title: Why sparse is not automatically faster
paragraphs: Dense matrix multiplication is easy to batch efficiently. Conditional routing adds selection, dispatch, variable batch sizes, and recombination. If only a few tokens reach an expert, its matrix operations may poorly utilize the hardware. Communication can dominate when experts live on different devices. Compare latency and throughput at realistic batch sizes, rather than inferring speed from active parameters alone. Also distinguish token-level sparsity from pruning: routing chooses a computation path dynamically, whereas pruning usually removes or masks components according to a different rule.

sections.title: Reading the original paper
paragraphs: Read the sparsely gated MoE paper and Mixtral with two ledgers open: one for parameters stored and another for expert computations executed by a token. Mark which parts of the model are shared before counting the routed branches. This prevents the phrase sparse model from being confused with a matrix whose elements are mostly zero or with a model that stores only its active experts.

Take the eight-expert example here and imagine a batch whose tokens collectively visit every expert. Per-token execution remains sparse while the batch touches the complete expert collection. Ask what that means for weight residency, batching, and device placement before translating an active-parameter count into a speed prediction. When reading experimental comparisons, identify whether the baseline is matched by total parameters, active computation, training budget, or measured latency. Each condition isolates a different question, and none can silently substitute for the others.

exercise.prompt: An MoE layer has six equal experts and activates two. What fraction of expert parameters is active per token, and what is still stored?
exercise.answer: One third is active per token. All six experts still need storage somewhere unless a separate loading or offloading strategy is used.

takeaways: Conditional execution decouples stored capacity from per-token expert work.
Sparse arithmetic can still have dense storage and communication costs.

title: What an expert actually computes
summary: In a common Transformer MoE design, an expert is a feed-forward network that preserves the residual-stream width.

sections.title: Replace a sublayer, not the entire model
paragraphs: An expert is usually an MLP or gated MLP. It receives a token representation and returns another vector of the same residual width. A router selects which experts process that token. This often replaces the dense FFN sublayer while attention, normalization, and residual connections remain shared. The term expert does not imply a separate language model or a human-labeled specialty. Its role emerges from optimization and the tokens it receives.

sections.title: Track the internal expansion
paragraphs: For a simple expert, input x has width d. A first projection expands it to h, a nonlinearity transforms it, and a second projection maps it back to d. The two matrices contain approximately 2dh parameters, excluding biases. Gated experts may use three projections and therefore different parameter counts. Regardless of internal width, the returned vector must match the expected residual dimension so that the routed output can be combined with the layer input.
sections.formula: Expert(x) = W₂ φ(W₁x); W₁ ∈ ℝ^(h×d), W₂ ∈ ℝ^(d×h)

sections.title: Build the smallest useful prototype
paragraphs: Use four experts with d = 16 and h = 32. Each two-matrix expert has 1,024 weight parameters, so the collection has 4,096. Route a batch of token vectors, run only selected experts, and restore the original token order before the residual addition. A useful debugging test sends every token to one chosen expert and checks that the MoE contribution, before residual addition, equals the standalone MLP output multiplied by its gate weight. Exact equality to the unweighted MLP requires a gate of one. A frequent error is returning tokens in dispatch order, which silently mixes representations between sequence positions while leaving tensor shapes apparently valid.

sections.title: Reading the original paper
paragraphs: Inspect the expert sublayer in Switch or Mixtral before thinking about model-scale parameter counts. Identify its input width, internal expansion, nonlinearity or gate, and output width. The defining interface is that a selected expert returns a token representation compatible with the surrounding residual stream. An expert is not automatically a complete independent language model merely because it has its own weights.

Translate one diagram into a tiny tensor program on paper: four input tokens, two experts, and a recorded destination for each token. Group the rows by destination, apply the appropriate feed-forward computation, and restore their original positions. This exercise separates the expert's local function from the router and dispatcher. For a gated expert, count each distinct projection instead of using the two-matrix estimate unchanged. The architectural reading should end with a shape and parameter-count description precise enough that another implementation could reproduce the same sublayer interface.

exercise.prompt: If an expert expands from d = 64 to h = 128 and back, how many matrix parameters does it contain?
exercise.answer: 64 × 128 + 128 × 64 = 16,384, excluding biases. Four such experts store 65,536 matrix parameters.

takeaways: An expert commonly replaces the FFN, while attention remains shared.
Restoring token order is as important as matching output shapes.

title: How a router selects experts
summary: A router converts a token representation into scores that determine its expert assignments and mixture weights.

sections.title: Routing is a small learned decision
paragraphs: For a token vector x, a linear router can produce one logit per expert. A softmax turns these logits into nonnegative scores summing to one. A selection rule then chooses a limited set of experts. This is a local decision based on the representation available at that layer; contextual information may already be encoded in x by previous attention. The router is not generally reading raw words and assigning fixed dictionary categories.

sections.title: Separate probabilities and discrete selection
paragraphs: Let R have shape [E, d]. Then Rx has E scores, and softmax(Rx) defines probabilities p. Top-k selection chooses indices, while selected scores may weight expert outputs. The index selection is discrete, but gradients can still reach selected gate values through the weighted output; auxiliary objectives provide additional training signals. Exact gradient paths depend on the implementation. Treating top-k indices as an ordinary smooth function is a conceptual mistake when reasoning about optimization.

sections.title: Inspect a concrete routing distribution
paragraphs: Suppose a router produces probabilities [0.55, 0.25, 0.15, 0.05]. Using zero-based indexing, a top-two rule chooses experts at indices 0 and 1. If selected weights are renormalized, their weights become 0.6875 and 0.3125. If they are not, their total contribution remains scaled by 0.8. Those are different layer definitions. During debugging, log logits, selected indices, gate weights, and per-expert token counts. Extreme logits early in training can make assignments overly concentrated, while perfectly balanced counts alone do not prove that routing improves task quality.

sections.title: Reading the original paper
paragraphs: Compare the gate construction in the original sparse MoE paper with the selected-expert formulation in Switch. Write down three objects separately: all-expert logits, the selected indices, and the numerical weights that multiply expert outputs. A softmax over selected logits and a softmax over all logits followed by selection do not have the same output scale unless an appropriate renormalization is applied.

Use a four-expert example to inspect the gradient path. Once an index set is fixed, the selected numerical weights can still depend differentiably on router logits; changing the winning indices is a separate discrete event. If top-one weights are renormalized to one, that particular mixture-magnitude gradient disappears. Ask how the studied system trains its router under the actual convention rather than assuming every top-k operator behaves identically. This reading approach connects the paper's equation to the optimization behavior that a seemingly small implementation change can alter.

exercise.prompt: For probabilities [0.2, 0.5, 0.3], which experts does top-two select, and what are their renormalized weights?
exercise.answer: The experts at zero-based indices 1 and 2, namely the second and third experts with probabilities 0.5 and 0.3. Their selected mass is 0.8, so the weights are 0.625 and 0.375.

takeaways: Routing scores, selected indices, and mixture weights are distinct objects.
Check the exact gradient and normalization conventions in your implementation.

title: Top-1, top-2, and top-k routing
summary: The number of selected experts trades per-token expert work against the richness of conditional computation.

sections.title: k controls how many paths are opened
paragraphs: Top-1 routing sends a token to one expert; top-2 sends it to two; top-k generalizes the same idea. Selecting several experts allows their outputs to contribute jointly, but it increases expert evaluations and dispatch traffic. The best k is not determined independently of expert size, number of experts, capacity limits, and training budget. Two small experts may cost less than one large expert, so comparisons should report actual dimensions.

sections.title: Count assignments rather than tokens
paragraphs: For T tokens with exactly k assignments each, the router creates kT token-expert assignments before overflow handling. With E balanced experts, each receives about kT/E assignments. These counts matter for capacity buffers and batching. A token routed twice must eventually have both outputs combined at its original position. Some systems enforce different routing constraints or drop overflow assignments, so the realized number of expert evaluations may differ from the nominal kT.
sections.formula: Assignments = kT; balanced assignments per expert = kT/E

sections.title: Understand the top-one normalization trap
paragraphs: With top-one selection, renormalizing the sole selected probability to one removes its magnitude from the output. Retaining the original probability preserves a gate multiplier and its associated gradient path. Both definitions can be implemented, but they are not identical. For a toy experiment with four experts, compare top-one and top-two while recording task loss, routing counts, and time. Do not only report the number of experts: a model with many experts and k = 1 has a very different per-token workload from one with the same expert count and k = 4.

sections.title: Reading the original paper
paragraphs: Switch and Mixtral are useful contrasting sources because their sparse layers choose different numbers of experts per token. Read their routing definitions alongside their expert dimensions. A count of one versus two says how many branches are selected, but it does not fully specify the amount of arithmetic, the amount of shared computation, or the dispatch buffer sizes.

Build a comparison with 100 tokens and first count assignments for each k before estimating expert work. Then change expert width so that two narrow branches approximately match one wide branch's matrix cost. The resulting architectures still differ in routing flexibility and communication, even under that arithmetic constraint. When interpreting a paper's speed result, look for batch size, hardware, capacity policy, and expert utilization. A useful ablation isolates k while making these costs visible; simply copying a published top-k setting into a differently sized model does not reproduce the original comparison.

exercise.prompt: A batch has 120 tokens, six experts, and top-two routing. Under perfect balance, how many assignments reach each expert?
exercise.answer: There are 240 assignments, so each expert receives 40. The number of distinct input tokens is still 120.

takeaways: k changes assignments, compute, and communication together.
State whether selected gate weights are renormalized.

title: Combining expert outputs correctly
summary: An MoE layer must weight selected expert outputs and scatter them back into the original token positions.

sections.title: A mixture is a weighted sum
paragraphs: After dispatch, each selected expert returns a vector with the residual-stream width. The layer combines those vectors using router-derived weights. This lets one token draw on several computations without concatenating their widths. If outputs have dimension d, the weighted sum also has dimension d. The router weight is a scalar per token-expert assignment, usually broadcast across features. Averaging the outputs unconditionally would discard information encoded in the learned gate values.

sections.title: Work through a small vector example
paragraphs: Let expert one return [2, 0] and expert two return [0, 4], with normalized weights 0.75 and 0.25. The mixture is [1.5, 1]. Concatenation would instead give a four-dimensional vector and would not match the ordinary residual interface. If unnormalized selected weights are used, the output magnitude also depends on their total probability mass. Gradients through the sum update both selected expert computations and any differentiable gate weights.
sections.formula: y_t = Σ over selected e g_t,e E_e(x_t)

sections.title: Dispatch order must not become sequence order
paragraphs: A batched implementation often groups assignments by expert for efficient matrix multiplication. Maintain the original token index and gate weight beside every dispatched row. Multiply each returned row by its weight and scatter-add it into an output buffer indexed by the original token. Scatter-add matters because one token may receive several contributions. A simple assignment operation can overwrite earlier expert outputs. Validate the optimized implementation against a slow loop over tokens and selected experts, including repeated indices, empty experts, and noncontiguous inputs.

sections.title: Reading the original paper
paragraphs: The gated-sum equations in sparse MoE papers specify a function, while a dispatcher implements that function through reordered batches. Keep those two levels separate while reading. First compute a token's mixture directly from expert outputs and scalar gate weights. Only then reorganize the calculation into expert-specific batches, carrying the token index and mixture weight with every dispatched row.

Consider two tokens that each select the same two experts. The return operation must combine two contributions for each original token without combining contributions between tokens. Write down the four dispatch rows and their destination indices; an ordinary overwrite would lose a valid term even though all tensor dimensions match. Use this toy construction to interpret any optimized implementation associated with the paper. Agreement with the direct gated sum is the relevant correctness condition, while faster grouping or communication is a separate systems improvement that should preserve that condition.

exercise.prompt: Two expert outputs are [1, 3] and [5, 1], with weights 0.4 and 0.6. What is the mixture?
exercise.answer: 0.4[1, 3] + 0.6[5, 1] = [3.4, 1.8]. Both contributions must be added to the same token's output.

takeaways: Mixture weights multiply complete expert output vectors.
Use scatter-add when several assignments return to one token.

title: Why load balancing needs its own objective
summary: A router can optimize task loss while starving some experts, so utilization must be monitored and sometimes regularized.

sections.title: Positive feedback can concentrate traffic
paragraphs: An expert that receives more tokens gets more opportunities to improve. Better performance may then cause the router to send it even more tokens. Other experts can receive little training and remain uncompetitive. This is one possible form of expert collapse. Balancing objectives encourage broader utilization, but uniform traffic is a means to improve training and system efficiency, not the final learning goal. Real token distributions may legitimately have unequal difficulty.

sections.title: Connect assignments and probabilities
paragraphs: A common top-one balancing term uses f_e, the fraction of tokens assigned to expert e, and P_e, the mean routing probability for e across the batch. The product sum penalizes concentration when assignment frequency and probability mass align. Let N_E denote the number of experts. A coefficient λ sets the strength of this auxiliary loss relative to the task loss. Assignment counts are discrete, while the probability averages provide a differentiable path. This specific form is only one design; other routers use different balancing mechanisms.
sections.formula: L_balance = N_E Σₑ fₑ Pₑ; L_total = L_task + λ L_balance

sections.title: Interpret the scale with a toy case
paragraphs: For four experts under uniform routing, f_e = P_e = 0.25, giving L_balance = 1. If all tokens and probability mass go to one expert, the value is 4. The coefficient therefore matters: a large coefficient can prioritize equal traffic at the expense of useful specialization. Track both the auxiliary term and the main task metric, along with per-expert counts and dropped assignments. Do not diagnose health from the mean probability alone; an apparently smooth mean can hide very uneven hard selections or imbalances across devices.

sections.title: Reading the original paper
paragraphs: In the Switch paper, inspect the definitions of hard assignment frequency and average router probability before using the auxiliary objective. They are not two names for the same statistic. One records which expert wins a selection rule, while the other preserves the distribution of soft scores across the batch. That distinction explains why a smooth average probability can coexist with uneven hard routing.

Recalculate the uniform example and a concentrated example from this article, including the external coefficient when combining with task loss. The value one is the stated uniform reference, not a probability of correctness or a reason to optimize the auxiliary term in isolation. Examine per-expert counts, token overflow, and task performance together when assessing the paper's balancing strategy. A useful independent experiment holds the router probabilities nearly tied and changes a small logit bias: hard assignments can shift sharply even when the mean scores barely move, exposing why both measurements matter.

exercise.prompt: With two experts, f = [0.75, 0.25] and P = [0.6, 0.4], what is this balancing term?
exercise.answer: 2 × (0.75 × 0.6 + 0.25 × 0.4) = 1.1. Its contribution to total loss is this value multiplied by the chosen coefficient.

takeaways: Inspect hard assignments and soft probability mass together.
Balance is an optimization constraint, not proof of semantic specialization.

title: Capacity limits and dropped assignments
summary: Expert capacity bounds the number of token assignments processed in a routing group, creating an accuracy–resource trade-off.

sections.title: Balanced averages do not prevent overload
paragraphs: Even if routing is balanced on average, one batch may send too many tokens to a particular expert. Systems often allocate a fixed capacity per expert to keep memory and computation predictable. A capacity factor multiplies the expected balanced load. The exact denominator and routing group depend on the implementation, especially with top-k routing and distributed batches. Always define whether capacity is measured in tokens, assignments, or per-device dispatch slots.

sections.title: Compute the buffer requirement
paragraphs: In a simple assignment-based convention, capacity C = ceil(c kT/E), where c is the factor, T the token count, E the expert count, and k the selected experts per token. For T = 64, E = 4, k = 1, and c = 1.25, C is 20. If one expert receives 25 assignments, five overflow its buffer. A top-two system would need to account for twice as many assignments under this convention.

sections.title: Overflow is a model behavior
paragraphs: Overflow assignments may be dropped, rerouted, or handled with a dropless implementation. Dropping an expert contribution does not necessarily delete the token from the model: a shared residual path may still carry its representation. Nevertheless, the intended expert computation is missing. Log the overflow rate and investigate which examples are affected. A training setup that drops tokens heavily can create differences from a deployment setup with larger capacity. Increasing capacity reduces overflow but can reserve more memory and may increase padding or scheduling costs.

sections.title: Reading the original paper
paragraphs: Use Switch's expert-capacity discussion to locate the boundary between a mathematical router and a system with finite buffers. For a chosen routing group, list the input-token count, number of assignments per token, number of experts, and capacity convention. The same numerical capacity factor can imply different buffer sizes if an implementation uses a different group or counts top-k assignments differently.

Draw a dispatch table where one expert is overloaded and another has spare slots. Uniform total capacity does not automatically move work between them; that requires an explicit overflow policy. Mark which expert contributions are missing after dropping and trace what still reaches the next layer through a residual path. When reading quality or speed comparisons, check whether capacity changes between training and evaluation. Dropless processing is an alternative systems design, not something implied by the capacity-factor formula, and it can exchange dropped work for different batching, memory, or scheduling costs.

exercise.prompt: An expert has capacity 18 and receives 23 assignments. What fraction overflows if excess assignments are dropped?
exercise.answer: 5/23 ≈ 21.7% of that expert's incoming assignments overflow. This is not necessarily the percentage of original tokens removed from the sequence.

takeaways: Define capacity using the implementation's actual routing group.
Measure overflow explicitly and distinguish dropped work from deleted tokens.

title: Testing whether experts specialize
summary: Expert specialization is a hypothesis about learned behavior that requires more evidence than an interesting routing plot.

sections.title: Traffic patterns are only a first clue
paragraphs: An expert may receive many numerical tokens, code fragments, or words from one language. That pattern suggests a possible specialization, but it does not prove that the expert uniquely performs arithmetic, programming, or translation. Token frequency, position, formatting, and dataset composition can produce similar patterns. Because representations are contextual, the same surface token can route differently in different sentences or layers. Treat expert names as descriptive labels for an analysis, not as intrinsic model properties.

sections.title: Measure distributions with controls
paragraphs: Collect routing counts for token categories while also recording their base frequencies. If 60% of an expert's traffic is code, compare that with the percentage of code in the entire evaluation set. Normalize counts and examine several layers and seeds. Conditional probabilities answer different questions: P(category|expert) describes traffic composition, whereas P(expert|category) describes routing preference. Neither alone measures whether the expert is necessary for the corresponding capability.
sections.formula: P(category|expert) and P(expert|category) answer different questions

sections.title: Use interventions carefully
paragraphs: A stronger test masks, replaces, or reroutes an expert and measures which tasks degrade. Compare against random expert removal at a matched compute change, since disabling any useful capacity can hurt performance. For a small model, train on two synthetic distributions and inspect whether specialized routing predicts which expert interventions matter. Also check stability: an apparent specialization that changes completely across seeds may reflect interchangeable solutions. Avoid assuming that equal load and sharp semantic specialization can always be achieved simultaneously; their objectives may sometimes compete.

sections.title: Reading the original paper
paragraphs: Read the routing analysis in Mixtral and the specialization experiments in DeepSeekMoE as evidence with different strengths. A traffic visualization reveals association; removing or changing experts can reveal functional sensitivity, but also changes available capacity and input distributions. Neither observation alone gives an expert a fixed human-readable job description. Begin by identifying exactly what was measured and what alternative explanation remains.

Create a two-way table of expert assignments and token categories. From that one table, calculate both category-given-expert and expert-given-category distributions, keeping category base rates visible. Then design a matched intervention: remove a candidate expert and compare the task effect with removing another expert under similar compute conditions. A selective degradation is more informative than an attractive category label. Repeat the analysis across layers or data mixtures, because a specialization claim should specify where and under which distribution it holds rather than implying a permanent property of an expert index.

exercise.prompt: An expert receives 70% code tokens, while the whole dataset is 80% code. Does that alone show a code preference?
exercise.answer: No. Relative to the dataset baseline, its traffic is less code-heavy. You need normalized routing statistics and ideally a controlled intervention.

takeaways: Compare routing patterns against dataset base rates.
Use matched interventions to test whether a specialization is causally useful.

title: Counting total and active parameters
summary: Total parameters describe stored model capacity, while active parameters describe a token's selected computation path.

sections.title: Include shared components in both counts
paragraphs: An MoE model contains shared components such as attention, embeddings, normalization, and possibly shared experts. Routed experts add a larger collection of conditionally used parameters. Total parameter count includes all of them. Active parameter count usually includes shared parameters plus the selected experts for one token, but reporting conventions can differ around embeddings and output heads. State your convention explicitly rather than comparing two headline numbers as if they were automatically identical measurements.

sections.title: Derive a simple model count
paragraphs: Let P_shared be shared parameters and let E equal-sized experts each contain P_expert parameters. If each token selects k experts, total count is P_shared + E P_expert and active count is approximately P_shared + k P_expert. With 20 million shared parameters and eight experts of ten million each, the total is 100 million. Selecting two gives 40 million active parameters. This arithmetic does not include routing overhead or account for actual FLOPs per parameter.
sections.formula: P_total = P_shared + E P_expert; P_active ≈ P_shared + k P_expert

sections.title: Per-token and per-batch activity differ
paragraphs: One token may activate two experts, while a batch collectively touches every expert. Consequently, batching can improve utilization without reducing the need to store the full collection. Active parameters also do not uniquely determine latency: sequence length changes attention work, and communication changes device time. When comparing a dense and sparse model, report total storage, active parameter convention, measured FLOPs if available, batch size, and latency or throughput. A claim that an MoE model is equivalent to a dense model of its active size is too strong; their capacity and computation structure differ.

sections.title: Reading the original paper
paragraphs: Use Mixtral's distinction between total and active parameters as a prompt to reconstruct the counts, not just repeat the headline values. Separate shared attention and other common components from the routed expert collection. Then identify the reporting convention for embeddings and output projections. Parameter storage, parameter use by one token, and floating-point operations are related but different accounting quantities.

Apply the formula to a complete hypothetical stack rather than one isolated layer. Count how many layers actually contain experts and whether their widths or routing counts vary. A batch that visits all experts can still have a small active count per token, so the active number does not bound the batch's resident model storage. When comparing with a dense model, ask what claim the matching count supports. Equal active parameters is not a proof of equal latency, equal learned capacity, or equal quality; each of those needs an additional measurement or assumption.

exercise.prompt: A model has 30M shared parameters and twelve 5M experts. With top-three routing, what are total and active counts?
exercise.answer: Total: 30 + 12 × 5 = 90M. Active per token: 30 + 3 × 5 = 45M, under the stated shared-plus-selected convention.

takeaways: Shared parameters contribute to both total and active counts.
Per-token activity does not describe the entire batch's memory footprint.

title: Expert parallelism and the communication bill
summary: Distributing experts saves per-device storage but requires moving token representations to the devices that own them.

sections.title: Put the network around the computation
paragraphs: Expert parallelism assigns different experts to different devices. After routing, each token representation must reach the selected expert's device, and its output must return to the original sequence owner. This exchange is often implemented with collective communication such as all-to-all. It differs from ordinary data parallelism, where each device has a model replica and processes different examples. Real systems can combine expert, tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism, making the communication pattern more complex.

sections.title: Estimate payload before timing it
paragraphs: For T input tokens, k selected experts per token, hidden width d, and b bytes per activation value, a simple payload estimate is kTdb bytes for dispatch and a similar amount for returning outputs. With T = 1024, k = 2, d = 2048, and b = 2, one direction contains about 8.39 MB of activation values. This is not a complete network-traffic prediction: local assignments, metadata, padding, topology, and collective algorithms change what actually crosses links.

sections.title: Small expert batches can waste hardware
paragraphs: Communication is only one bottleneck. Uneven routing makes some devices finish late, and tiny per-expert batches reduce matrix-multiplication efficiency. Increasing global batch size may help utilization but can change latency and optimization. Profile dispatch, expert computation, combine, and synchronization separately. Compare balanced synthetic routing with real routing to reveal load-related stalls. A common mistake is benchmarking experts in isolation and reporting that speed as end-to-end MoE speed; it omits exactly the routing and transfer costs that determine whether distribution is worthwhile.

sections.title: Reading the original paper
paragraphs: Read GShard's expert dispatch and resharding discussion alongside the original sparse MoE paper. Trace a token representation from its original device to its selected expert and back. In GShard, inspect the change from a token-partitioned layout to an expert-partitioned layout and identify the AllToAll operation that connects them. Count activation values moved, not only weights held by each device. This connects conditional computation to a concrete distributed execution plan.

Use the payload estimate in this article with a clearly defined T: input tokens before top-k replication. Separate logical dispatched bytes from bytes that cross a physical link, since local assignments need no remote transfer and collective implementations can introduce their own costs. Then consider an uneven routing batch: the total payload can stay similar while one device becomes a bottleneck. Reading efficiency results with this distinction helps explain why isolated expert throughput cannot stand in for end-to-end performance, and why topology, overlap, padding, and token distribution belong in the experiment description.

exercise.prompt: If k doubles while token count, hidden width, and dtype stay fixed, what happens to the simple dispatch payload estimate?
exercise.answer: It doubles. Real latency need not double because bandwidth, local routing, overlap, and fixed collective overhead also affect execution.

takeaways: Expert parallelism trades device storage for token movement.
Profile dispatch and recombination as well as expert matrix operations.

title: Three ways to design a sparse expert model
summary: Switch, Mixtral, and DeepSeekMoE illustrate different choices about routing, expert granularity, and shared computation.

sections.title: Compare design decisions rather than names
paragraphs: Switch emphasizes a simple top-one routing design. Mixtral uses top-two routing in its sparse expert layers. DeepSeekMoE explores finer-grained routed experts together with shared experts. These choices address related but distinct questions: how many paths to activate, how to divide expert capacity, and which computation should be available to every token. The model families also differ in training data and architecture, so their benchmark differences cannot be attributed solely to the routing rule.

sections.title: Normalize a hypothetical comparison
paragraphs: Imagine a budget of eight large experts, with two activated per token. Splitting each large expert into several narrower experts changes the number of combinations a router can choose, but preserving active computation requires adjusting how many smaller experts are selected. Adding a shared expert further changes the common workload. Count shared parameters, routed parameters, selected expert widths, and communication separately. Equal total parameters do not ensure equal active FLOPs, while equal active parameters do not ensure equal latency.

sections.title: Turn the designs into an ablation
paragraphs: Build a small controlled model and first compare top-one versus top-two at matched active compute. Next, compare coarse and fine expert partitions, then add shared expert capacity while adjusting the routed budget. Record validation loss, load balance, overflow, throughput, and specialization diagnostics. Change one design choice at a time where possible. Avoid claiming that one named architecture universally dominates: the value of routing simplicity, flexible combinations, or shared computation depends on the task distribution and the hardware that executes it.

sections.title: Reading the original paper
paragraphs: Read Switch, Mixtral, and DeepSeekMoE through a common worksheet rather than a sequence of benchmark rankings. Record selected experts per token, expert hidden width, routed expert count, shared computation, and balancing or capacity policy. The named systems bundle several choices together. A difference in their final score cannot identify which individual choice caused it when data and training conditions also change.

For a controlled design exercise, split one wide feed-forward expert into smaller candidate experts and adjust the number selected so the approximate active matrix work stays fixed. Then allocate part of that work to an always-available shared expert. Ask which routing combinations become possible and which costs remain shared. The DeepSeekMoE reading motivates those axes, while Switch and Mixtral illustrate different routing simplifications. Such a worksheet turns the papers into a space of testable designs, with storage, arithmetic, and communication constraints stated explicitly instead of treating one architecture name as a universally optimal answer.

exercise.prompt: Why is comparing two MoE models at equal total parameters insufficient to isolate a routing improvement?
exercise.answer: They may activate different numbers or sizes of experts, use different shared capacity, and incur different communication. Match active computation and training conditions as well.

takeaways: Compare routing count, expert granularity, and shared computation separately.
Use controlled ablations to distinguish architecture choices from training differences.
